# 6th International Conference on Applied Human Factors and Ergonomics (AHFE 2015) and the Affiliated Conferences, AHFE 2015

# Trust in automation – Before and after the experience of take-over scenarios in a highly automated vehicle

Christian Gold $^{a,*}$ , Moritz Körber $^{a}$ , Christoph Hohenberger $^{b}$ , David Lechner $^{a}$ , Klaus Bengler $^{a}$

$^{a}$ Institute of Ergonomics, Technische Universität München, Boltzmannstraße 15, 85748 Garching bei München, Germany  
 $^{b}$ Technische Universität München, Arcisstraße 21, 80333 München, Germany

## Abstract

Highly automated vehicles (Level 3, [1]) are likely to enter the market within the next decade. By removing the driver from the driver-vehiclesystem, positive impacts, for instance on road-safety or fuel consumption, are expected. These predicted effects can only arise if automated vehicles are accepted by society. Trust as well as the attitude towards technology has been found to be a precursor in the acceptance formation process. Therefore, we conducted a driving simulator experiment within the interdisciplinary research group at the Munich Center of Technology in Society (MCTS) in order to investigate how the experience of automated driving will change trust in automation and the attitude of the driver towards automation. The sample consisted of 72 participants between 19 and 79 years (M=44.97, SD=22.16). Participants completed a questionnaire before and after the driving simulator experience to assess trust in automation, safety gain, intention to use and other constructs in order to analyze the change caused by the driving simulation experience. Besides participants' ratings from the questionnaires, their gaze behavior was recorded in order to measure a change of trust by a change in scanning behavior. The participants drove highly automated on a three lane highway ata speed of 120 km/h. As critical situations are expected to have a significant impact on trust in automation, the participants experienced three take-over scenarios (system limits). Results indicate that the driving experience increased self-reported trust in automation and lead to a decrease in other measured constructs like safety gain. Older participants rated the vehicle automation more positively than younger drivers. Horizontal gaze behavior could not be confirmed as a metric for measuring trust in automation, although this measure behaved as expected and analogous to the self-reported level of trust.

## 1. Introduction

It is prospected that the replacement of the human in monotonous driving situations or in day-to-day traffic situations by an automated system could reduce accidents, increase road safety, increase driver's comfort and reduce emissions. This is not only dependent upon an accurate and sophisticated automated function, but also by the adaption of the driver and society. Only if those systems are broadly accepted and used, can they unfold their potential benefits. The decision whether to use an automated function is dependent upon the trust in automation [2]. "If a machine or function is distrusted, the user will, if possible, do the task(s) himself" [3]. Data of Lee and Moray [4] show that "the operator's use of automatic controllers depends upon more than trust alone" and Parasuraman and Riley [2] conclude that "several authors have suggested that automation reliability and the operator's trust in automation are major factors". So does Muir [5]: "One important determination of operator's choice of manual or automatic control may be their degree of trust in the automation". Conversely, having too much trust in an automated function could lead to overreliance and further to misuse and disuse of the automation [2] and has a potential for complacency [6]. There is little known about trust in automated vehicles. However, those processes became relevant within the last couple of years, but studies often merely focus on functioning and controllability aspects of automation[9, 10, 11]. Examining processes that will affect trust in automated vehicles is complicated, as the design of future series vehicles' automation systemshas not been determined yet. Research has been shown that "system performance and the occurrence of faults affect trust" [4] as well as the "human's ability to estimate the predictability of the machine's behaviours" [3]. Therefore, trust in automation was rather investigated in domains like production processes or aviation where such systems are already in use. The only studies known to the authors that were conducted in an automotive context and that are comparable to automated driving look at trust in an ACC-system (e.g. [7, 8]) or in more general ADAS [12].

It is, therefore, important to investigate how trust in vehicle automation evolves in order to predict effects that may hamper or facilitate the acceptance of automated vehicles. For this purpose, a driving simulator experiment in the high fidelity driving simulator of the Institute of Ergonomics, Technische Universität München, was conducted.

## 2. Method

## 2.1. Procedure

In a driving simulation study, 72 participants experienced highly automated driving (HAD) within an approximately 15-20 minute drive that included three take-over situations. They had to complete a questionnaire before and after the drive to assess their attitude regarding HAD. After a short welcome, participants were briefed about the automated system, system limits, the driver's responsibilities in a highly automated vehicle and the procedure for the experiment. Regarding the system and its limits, participants were informed that the functioning of the automation is flawless and they do not have to monitor the system, but there will be situations the automation is not capable of solving. In such situations, the system emits a warning signal and they have to take over vehicle control again. After these instructions, participants had to complete the first questionnaire to indicate personal information like age and driving experience. This was followed by a short introductory drive to get familiar with the driving simulation and the vehicle automation. As soon as the participant felt comfortable and was able to handle the driving task and the functions of the vehicle, eye tracking hardware was calibrated and the main drive was started. After the drive task was completed, the second questionnaire was distributed.

## 2.2. Driving simulation

The study was conducted in a driving simulator that was implemented by a BMW Series-6 full vehicle mockup, which was surrounded by seven projectors that enable a front view of about 180 degrees and the use of all three mirrors. Road and engine noise are played back over the audio system of the mockup; light vibrations of low frequencies are also produced. The activated automation took over longitudinal and lateral vehicle control and could also perform lane changes. The automation could be switched on by pressing a button on the active steering wheel and switched off bypassing the same button or any steering or braking input. The central information displayindicated automation state by green (on) and red (off/take-over) symbols. The take-over requests (TOR) were presented by thered symbol and a sharp double earcon(3000 Hz; 74 dB), similar to ACC collision warnings in current vehicles. Participants were able to talk to the experimenter via an intercom system.

## 2.3. Take-over situations

The TORs were triggered by a stranded vehicle on the participant's current lane. Participants were warned seven seconds in advance of the potential collision. In order to handle these situations, participants had to regain control and brake or steer to change lanes and avoid the collision. As this was a combined study also examining the influence of traffic density on the take-over performance, three different traffic densities (0, 10, 20 vehicles/km) on the lanes next to the ego vehicle were implemented. Influences of traffic density on take-over performance are reported in a future study. The lane in which the take-over situation occurred changed with each subsequent situation for each participant.

## 2.4. Experimental variables

Next to the factors traffic density and lane, which are not part of this study, half of the participants had to engage in a non-driving related task called a 20-Questions-Task. Data analysis of the influence of a secondary task will be presented in another article in the future.

Several studies suggest that age influences trust in automation [14] and older adults rely more on automation [15] and are more sensitive to changes in automation's reliability [16]. Therefore, the participants were recruited from different age groups to be able to depict age effects in a between-subject design. Half of the participants $(N = 36)$ were below 30 years, the other half above 60 years old.

The main dependent variables in this study were subjective evaluations regarding the perception of the HAD before and after the simulation. In both questionnaires, we asked for the perceived discharge of the driver due to automation, safety gain, safety hazard, trust in automation, perceived control of conduct and intention of use (see Appendix A).

The questionnaire was presented in the German language and its questions retrieved from the article of Jian, Bisantz, and Drury [18] were translated into German in cooperation with an American native speaker.

Besides the questionnaires, eye tracking data was recorded. Several studies already indicated that the workload of the driver can be objectively measured by eyetracking parameters like horizontal gaze deviation  $[19,20,21]$ . He and his colleagues  $[22]$  found that mind wandering behind the wheel leads to a decrease in horizontal gaze deviations. In more general terms, gaze behavior is an indicator for situation awareness. Moore and Gugerty  $[23]$  for example found a relationship between the fixation time on relevant areas of interest as well as the gaze distribution and the number of errors made by operators. Ratwani, McCurry and Trafton $[24]$  identified visual scanning to be a strong predictor of situation awareness. Regarding trust in automation, Moray  $[25]$  stated that an observer is complacent if he monitors a source less frequently. Based on these findings, we expect that gaze distribution and scanning behavior are related to trust in automation. Participants who mistrust the automated vehicle are expected to stay aware of the driving scene, check mirrors and show a similar scanning behavior as in manual driving; whereas drivers with a high level of trust in automation will be more likely to allocate attention away from the driving task showing a decrease in scanning behavior and beginning tomind wander. Mistrust is expected to lead to reduced scanning and high standard deviation of horizontal gaze distribution, whereas high levels of trust should increase this measure. Furthermore, age-related effects are expected to be found in gaze behavior since older drivers show significantly different scanning behavior while driving  $[26]$ .

The horizontal gaze deviation was chosen as a promising metric since it is seen as the most effective metric for measuring workload  $[19]$  and, therefore, is sensitive to the narrowing of scanning and a lower rate in checking mirrors, objects and displays. Its resulting data is dependent upon the setting as it is measured in pixels within the eye tracking video. To see whether horizontal gaze deviation changed due to the automated drive, we analyzed the gaze data of the first and the last minute of the experiment. If trust can be measured by horizontal gaze deviation, the difference between these two data points should correlate with the difference between these two points in self-reported trust. Figure 1 shows a comparison of the gaze behavior of two different subjects that we recorded during the experiment.

## 3. Results

For all statistical tests, a significance level of $\alpha = .05$ was set. The 72 participants had a mean age of 44.97 years ($SD = 22.16$), whereas the young group had a mean age of 23.28 years ($SD = 2.60$) and the elderly group had a mean age of 66.67 years ($SD = 4.56$). Older drivers in this study have a higher average mileage driven($\chi^2(3) = 24.64$, $p < .001$) than younger drivers (see Figure 2). Two participants from the young drivers group were excluded from the analysis since they closed their eyes for more than 20 seconds within one minute during data recording. Another participant of the elderly group did not react to one of the TORs, although it was clearly audible. Therefore, the sample for data analysis consisted of 69 participants.

## 3.1. Questionnaires

To analyze the questionnaire data, we conducted a mixed-design analysis of variance (ANOVA) with the repeated measures and the within factor repetition (2 levels) and a between-subject factor age group (2 levels). We found significant differences in the group means for the factor repetition $(\mathrm{F}(1,67) = 4.39, p = .001;)$ and age group $(\mathrm{F}(1,67) = 6.59, p < .001)$, however, no significant interaction effect could be reported $(\mathrm{F}(1;67) = 0.97, p = .462)$. Figure 3 shows the results (error bars represent standard deviation) and significant differences of post-hoc pairwise comparisons (Bonferroni). Discharge of the driver due to automation $(t(67) = 2.19, p = .032)$ and safety gain $(t(67) = 2.46, p = .039)$ differ significantly between the first and second questionnaire. Trust shows a tendency to increase but is only close to being significant $(t(67) = -1.92, p = .060)$. Contrary to the ratings of discharge of the driver due to automation and safety gain, which decreased, trust in automation increased. Data shows a significant difference in the ratings between young and elderly drivers in safety gain $(t(67) = -2.95, p = 0.004)$, trust $(t(67) = -2.62, p = 0.011)$, perceived control of conduct $(t(67) = -4.58, p < .001)$ and intention to use $(t(67) = -2.94, p = .004)$. Compared to younger drivers, elderly drivers show more trust and higher ratings regarding the other attributes.

## 3.2. Eyetracking

Horizontal gaze deviation was analyzed as a potential measurement of trust in automation.Data revealed a small difference $(d = 0.11)$ in horizontal gaze deviation in the elderly participants between the first $(M = 73.71, SD = 36.73)$ and the last minute $(M = 68.02, SD = 32.34)$ of the experiment. The same effect can be seen in the younger participants, as horizontal gaze deviation changed from 100.54 $(SD = 39.38)$ in the first minute to 86.91 $(SD = 33.09)$ and in the last minute $(d = 0.38)$.This difference is significant at our chosen significance level $(t(67) = 2.99, p = .004)$ as well as the difference between the two age groups $(t(67) = 2.94, p = .005)$.

## 3.3. Correlations of dependent variables

Unintentionally, car crashes occurred within the experimental scenario. In the young group, 4 out of 34 and 7 out of 35 in the elderly group could not avoid a crash with ether the car triggering the system limit or the vehicles on the neighboring lane. One-sided correlations (Spearman) were calculated in order to capture correlations between crash involvement and the ratings in the second questionnaire (see Table 1). In order to validate horizontal gaze deviation as a trust measurement, we also calculated a correlation between crash involvement and the change in horizontal gaze deviation between first and second measurement point (see Table 1). Horizontal gaze deviation in the beginning of the experiment and trust in automation measured in the first questionnaire show a correlation coefficient (Spearman) of $r = .08$ ($p = .260$, 1-tailed). Between the measures at the second measuring point data show a correlation coefficient (Spearman) of $r = -.09$ ($p = .237$, 1-tailed).

## 4. Discussion

Two participants fell asleep or at least closed their eyes for periods of several seconds, even after having experienced two take-over situations. This indicates a generally high level of trust in the system by these participants and probably a low arousal level. This corresponds with a high reported level of trust after the experiment of 5.15 on average on the 7-item Likert scale.

Another participant (elderly group) did not notice one of the TORs, although the TOR was designed according to the recommendations of NHTSA [27] for forward collision warning systems with a “flashing visual icon” and a 3000 Hz “urgent-sounding auditory signal [...] presented from a front speaker at around 75 dB” (p.81). The participant reported no impaired hearing capacity in the relevant questionnaire. Nevertheless, an age-related reduction of hearing capacity in combination with a current ongoing conversation with the experimenter over the intercom system may be the reason that the participant missed the signal.

In general, elderly subjects showed a more positive rating of the system and higher trust than the younger group. This finding is in accordance with past related work (e.g. [15]). Older drivers reported a higher gain in safety and a higher intention to use. The latter may result from a different life situation in people over 60 compared to people below 30 years of age, as questions included the willingness to buy, and financial circumstances of the group may differ. A similar influence of financial factors may affect the rating of perceived control of conduct; however, elderly participants are more likely to use such automated system than younger drivers.

Furthermore, discharge of the driver and safety gain are decreased in the course of the experiment while trust in automation is increased. The rating in the pre-experiment questionnaire is based on newspaper articles, reports in different media, hearsay and the short introduction to the experiment, but not on experience with the system. Expectations regarding discharge of the driver and safety gain seem to be lower than the driving simulation depicts. An increase in trust is likely to emerge since no malfunction or failures of controllers or sensors occurred at all and the occurrence of failures has a strong influence on trust in automation  $[14, 28]$ .

Witnessing a crash in a take-over situation does influence the ratings in the post experimental questionnaire. Expectedly, crash involvement is correlated with lower discharge of the driver, safety gain, trust in automation, perceived control and intention of use.

In accordance with the questionnaire, horizontal gaze deviations behave as expected: They decrease in the course of the experiment, indicating an increase in trust. Elderly subjects show a higher trust level and smaller horizontal gaze deviations. Unfortunately, no correlations were found between horizontal gaze deviation and self-reported trust in automation. A possible reason for this could be that the experimental setting led to underload, which promotes engagement in activities like visually exploring the driving simulator. Additionally, we observed that some participants fixated their visual attention on passing vehicles, first in the mirror and then in front of them. This behavior is not necessarily active monitoring of the automation and traffic, but could rather be a gaze pattern, triggered by moving objects within the field of view. Nevertheless, since we found no significant correlations with subjective ratings, horizontal gaze behavior could not be proven to be a valid measurement of trust in automation, although subjective ratings seem to fit gaze behavior.

## 4.1. Limitations

Unfortunately, it is unknown how well a vehicle automation system will perform, how often faults or system limits will occur or how predictable machine behavior will be. This may be the reason for the lack of studies known to the authors examining trust in Level 3 automated vehicles. Although the authors of this study used their experience in designing automated functions and HMI, this study can only indicate trends and tendencies, but it does not provide absolute statements regarding trust in automated vehicles. Furthermore, trust measured in a driving simulator experience may differ from trust generated from the experiences in real vehicles, especially sincere vehicles imply risk of personal harm. Beyond this, we cannot eliminate doubts that fatigue may have had an influence on the rating in the second questionnaire and the gaze behavior. Finally, as the focus was shifted to a large number of subjects, the contact with the automated system was rather short. Although this short contact showed a significant change of the assessment of the system, we cannot make statements about long-term use.

## 5. Summary

To investigate whether trust in automated vehicles changes due to the experience of vehicle automation, a driving simulator study with 72 participants from two different age groups (young and elderly drivers) was conducted. The experience of highly automated driving within a short driving simulator drive increased self-reported trust in automation and decreased the factors safety gain and discharge of the driver from the driving task. Age-related effects were found as elderly drivers showed higher trust in automation and higher ratings of the system than younger drivers. The expectation that horizontal gaze deviation can be established as a valid measurement of trust in automation was not supported by the data, although the results matched the expectations.
